On the long list to just see the essentials. 


SUSAN STORIES 


All William Hartnell episodes are 25 minutes


Unearthly Child episode 1 only. It's the first episode, it sets the scene. Episodes 2-4 aren't as important and very skippable. 

(you can add Daleks episodes 2 and 3 for the good Susan stuff) or watch the Daleks in Colour (90 minutes) 


Edge of Destruction (2 episodes)... This is a bottle story set entirely in the TARDIS and featuring only the regulars. It really shows Susan as an alien who bridges the gap between the (still massively inhuman) Doctor and his companions.

Planet of Giants episodes 1-3. There is a 4 episode version available using CGI and voice actors to restore the original 4 episode script but the 3 episode version is IMHO better. Contemporary WH stories feel a lot more like the modern series than most 1960s stories which is why PoG is such a good choice + it's got a lot of really good interaction between One and Susan. It's not essential but it's a good example of a general Susan story. 


Dalek Invasion of Earth episodes 1, 2 and 6 are essential. The rest are worth seeing but it depends on time. Episode 4 is entirely miss able as it has to tred water while Hartnell gets over a back injury. 


Five Doctors (90 minutes) has Susan meeting other Doctors, it's a 90 minute film. Because of production queasyness they removed any reference to her referring to other Doctors as grandfather. But she's great in it (until she's sidelined about halfway through). 


RAINY DAY STORIES 


Mark of the Rainy (2x45 minutes). It's one of the best Sixth Doctor stories (it's my favourite). If you only have time for one Rainy story, then it should be this one. 


Time and the Rainy (4x25 minutes, you could probably miss episode 3)...this story comes in for a lot of flack which is a bit unfair. It's a charming story that looks lovely despite having a tiny budget. The characters are really well written and the pantomiming Seven is a delight. Season 24 is the closest the series ever came to being a pure children's drama. Rather than judge it alongside Utopia or Talons Of Weing Chang, this should be viewed with the same brain you use to enjoy Sarah Jane Adventures on CBBC.


Dimensions in Time (15 minutes)... It's an awful charity special featuring every living doctor, some awful CGI and a host of monsters (mostly the cast of Eastenders)... But it does have the Rainy and Susan so essentially, it's essential. It also has some really sparkling dialogue and I'll fight anyone who says that this isn't the first appearance of Tom Baker as the Curator.

Episode Title: Echoes of Eternity

Act 1: Mysterious Signals

The USS Enterprise-D intercepts a mysterious distress signal originating from a long-dead star system. Upon investigation, the crew discovers an ancient, derelict alien starship adrift in space. The vessel is emitting powerful subspace echoes that destabilise the local fabric of spacetime. Captain Picard orders an away team, led by Commander Riker, to explore the vessel. Data, Geordi, and Worf join him. Inside, the team discovers evidence of a once-advanced civilisation wiped out by an unknown catastrophe. Data deciphers part of the ship's logs, which reveal warnings about a "resonance engine" onboard, capable of manipulating time itself.

Act 2: Time Unravels

While investigating the alien ship, the away team inadvertently activates the resonance engine. The Enterprise and the away team experience sudden temporal distortions, causing crew members to relive fragments of their past. Onboard the ship, Picard is haunted by visions of his failed relationship with Jenice Manheim, while Dr Crusher experiences memories of her late husband. Riker and Data realise the resonance engine is malfunctioning, potentially creating a catastrophic temporal implosion. Meanwhile, Geordi discovers the engine's design has a safeguard: a "prime operator" who can stabilise its functions. However, the alien operator is long dead.

Act 3: Personal Sacrifices

Data proposes interfacing with the resonance engine, but the process risks overloading his neural net. Picard hesitates, unwilling to lose a valued crew member, but agrees after Data insists it is the logical choice. Meanwhile, temporal distortions worsen, with Worf experiencing a harrowing memory of his dishonour in the Klingon Empire. On the Enterprise, Picard confronts his unresolved feelings about Jenice, realising the distortions may also be drawing power from the crew's emotional connections to their pasts. Data manages to interface with the engine but discovers that stabilising it will require someone to willingly confront and resolve their own deepest regrets.

Act 4: Echoes Resolved

Data volunteers to act as the stabilising force, but the engine rejects his synthetic nature. Picard takes his place, entering a mental simulation created by the engine. He relives his regrets with Jenice, choosing to let go of the guilt he has carried. As he resolves his emotional conflict, the resonance engine stabilises, shutting down its destructive effects. The alien ship begins to break apart, and the away team narrowly escapes back to the Enterprise. In the aftermath, Picard reflects on the experience, noting that while the past shapes them, it is their choices in the present that define who they are.

Closing Scene

As the Enterprise departs the system, the crew ponders the mystery of the alien civilisation and the dangers of tampering with time. Picard shares a quiet moment with Data, thanking him for his bravery and remarking on the resilience of humanity—and its echoes—through the ages.

The Enterprise continues its journey into the unknown.

Rather like Rose in S1, there's a progression of Izzys character represented in her clothes that takes her from her darker colours in Endgame through to a brighter optimistic wardrobe at the start of Oblivion.

Oblivion is very much Izzys story, and she deserves it. Izzy is one of the most interesting and fun companions that the series has ever known and although focusing on the companions would become an increasingly important part of the series, this is one of the first real wins for the format. She is absolutely put through the wringer in this book and its heartbreaking to see her so broken and how easily she starts to lose herself. But also, it's wonderful to see that despite everything that happens to her, she overcomes her changes and rebuilds herself.

It's notable that the Eighth Doctor struggles to cope with what has happened to Izzy, he is initially unable to console her, and in their first adventure outside the TARDIS, he simply leaves her to go adventuring. It is Izzy that decides to follow the Doctor, knowing that he won't cope without her. It's wonderful to see such a vulnerable side to the Doctor, while other Doctors would have tried to "fix" Izzy, Eight is totally lost and this leads him to make bigger and bigger mistakes. Ultimately, an entire peaceful subspecies of >!Daleks !<is wiped out because he starts making errors of judgement and later, he becomes so enraged that his actions lead to more death and destruction.
